newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-STANKOWSKI LEADS BY A STROKE HEADING INTO TWO-ROUND SUNDAY.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-STANKOWSKI LEADS BY A STROKE HEADING INTO TWO-ROUND SUNDAY.

text.p: Paul Stankowski shot a six-under-par 66 Saturday to take a slim one-stroke lead over Michael Bradley and John Huston heading into the final day of the Honda Classic.

Stankowski's two-round total of 11-under-par 133 at the TPC at Heron Bay gave him an even slighter margin than a normal one-shot lead would amount to heading into the final day because both the third and fourth rounds were to be played Sunday.

After Friday's round was washed out, tour officials, in agreement with the tournament sponsor, announced that the event would be shortened to 54 holes. But several hours later PGA Tour commissioner Tim Finchem reversed the decision and so the tournament will conclude with a 36-hole finale.

Although 74 players made the cut at one under par, just the 64 at two under or better will tee it up on Sunday, so as to get both rounds completed before darkness. The other 10 players will receive $3,015 in official money.

Huston and Bradley both shot rounds of 65. Lee Janzen (68), Greg Kraft (67), and Doug Martin (66) were another stroke back at nine under. Britain's Colin Montgomerie, who shot 68, was one of four players at eight under.
Stankowski, already a winner this year at the Hawaiian Open, had six birdies and no bogeys on Saturday.
"Tomorrow will be a long day. It'll be an endurance test more than anything. I'm not much of a physical specimen. I don't really work out, so my cardio-vascular is not in good shape," he admitted.
"I'm not looking forward to playing an all-day tournament, but I guess I'd better load up on pasta and pancakes and all the carbohydrates I can find."

Huston wasn't as concerned about the prospect of walking 36 holes. "Once you get into it, you don't think too much about it, especially if you've got a good rhythm going. I hope I can take momentum from today into both roudns tomorrow.
"I've been struggling, but I'm just a couple of 20-foot putts away from a really good year," said Huston.
Nearly everyone in the field agreed that it was a good decision to keep the event at 72 holes.
"It's a golf tournament, isn't it?" asked Montgomerie. "A 54-hole victory is never what you're looking for, though obviously you'd take it, but it doesn't mean as much as when win after 72 holes."
